analysis.one_liner: Requires Medicare and Medicaid nursing homes to staff a registered nurse 24 hours a day, every day.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or a vote and died in House committees when the Congress ended in January 1991.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make it a condition of taking Medicare and Medicaid patients that nursing facilities have a registered nurse on duty around the clock. Larger facilities would have to comply by January 1, 1991, and smaller ones by January 1, 1993. Facilities that genuinely cannot hire a nurse could get a waiver if their residents do not need that level of care. The bill was referred to two House committees, sent to their health subcommittees, and never advanced.
analysis.who_benefits: Nursing home residents, and the families who rely on those facilities, would gain a guarantee that a registered nurse is on site at all hours, including nights and weekends when problems are most likely to be caught late or handled by less-trained staff. Registered nurses would gain a source of demand for their skills.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Nursing home residents and their families

how_it_helps.text: Medicare skilled nursing facilities and Medicaid nursing facilities would have to use a registered nurse 24 hours a day, 7 days a week, as a condition of participating in the programs.
Facilities with at least 90 beds would have to meet the requirement by January 1, 1991; all other facilities by January 1, 1993, giving smaller homes more time to adjust.

The Secretary of Health and Human Services could waive the requirement for a facility that has made diligent efforts, including paying prevailing-market wages for registered nurses, and whose residents' physicians indicate none of them need registered nursing services in the meantime.

analysis.who_pays: Nursing facility operators would bear the cost of hiring registered nurses around the clock, an expense that flows partly through Medicare and Medicaid reimbursement and partly through what facilities charge. Rural or small facilities that struggle to attract nurses would depend on the waiver process.
analysis.who_pays_short: Nursing facility operators and program budgets

drawbacks.text: The staffing mandate raises facility operating costs, which nursing facilities could pass on to Medicare, Medicaid, and private-pay residents, putting pressure on program budgets and family payments.
The requirement is hardest for small and rural facilities in labor markets short of registered nurses; the bill answers this only with a case-by-case waiver, which could be slow and inconsistent.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit to residents is concrete: a registered nurse on site at all hours means falls, infections, and drug problems are more likely to be caught and treated quickly, which is exactly when licensed practical nurses and aides are least equipped to act alone. The cost falls on facilities and, through reimbursement, on taxpayers and private-pay families, and it is real, especially for rural homes that cannot fill nurse positions. The bill's waiver for facilities that cannot hire and do not need the coverage is a reasonable cushion, though enforcing 'diligent efforts' at prevailing wages would decide whether the waiver is a safety valve or a loophole. On balance this is a straightforward care-quality standard whose cost is modest relative to the risk it addresses.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to two House committees, which passed it down to their health subcommittees, where it sat with no hearing, no markup, and no vote until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Doug Walgren introduced the bill on March 23, 1989, and it was referred jointly to the House Ways and Means and Energy and Commerce Committees.
In mid-April 1989 the bill was sent to the health subcommittees of both committees, the Subcommittee on Health and the Subcommittee on Health and the Environment.
No cosponsors signed on, and no further action was taken before the 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Nursing facility operators are better off, since they avoided a 24-hour registered nurse staffing mandate and its costs, while nursing home residents gained nothing.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never reached a vote and drew no cosponsors, so the record shows no partisan split; it simply stalled after subcommittee referral.

industries.industry: Nursing facilities (Medicare skilled nursing and Medicaid nursing homes)
industries.note: The bill would require facilities to employ a registered nurse around the clock, raising operating costs for an industry that staffs nights and weekends with less-licensed personnel. The industry's cost saving is the residents' safety risk, so its interest runs against the public's here.

A 24-hour RN requirement would create steady demand for registered nurses in nursing facilities, including at prevailing wages as a condition for waivers. More nurses on site directly benefits residents.
